title: Addressing threats to validity in large dataset research

# Addressing threats to validity in large dataset research

PMC13726918. PLOS Medicine, 23(11):e1005282. Published 2026-11-02.

## Authors

Wonsuk Yoo, John P. A. Ioannidis

## Details

- DOI: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005282
- PMID: 42970497 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42970497/)
- PMCID: PMC13726918
- License: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

---

## Abstract

Large dataset research offers new opportunities across biomedicine, but it also faces major threats to validity. These threats are underappreciated and often not recognized or managed appropriately. We dissect here 4 major types of validity threats: (1) P-value inflation and trivial effects; (2) residual and differential confounding across multiple sites; (3) issues surrounding harmonization and measurement error; and (4) causal identification in the presence of rich covariates. For each of them we provide their theoretical background, empirical evidence, and simulations that showcase how they operate. We make recommendations that may offer guidance for analyses and inferences from large datasets across biomedicine. These include: deciding on the placement in a continuum of exploration versus targeted causation; evaluating both statistical significance and effect sizes; modeling site heterogeneity; treating harmonization as measurement modeling; considering causal diagrams to guide adjustment; checking covariate balance; embedding sensitivity analysis and exploration of robustness; reporting limitations structurally; considering falsification calibration of performance; considering multi-analyst approaches; enhancing sharing, openness, transparency, and documentation; and considering encompassing analyses rather than least publishable units. Improving large dataset research and adequately addressing these threats is essential for the integrity of the scientific record and eventually also for informing policy and clinical practice.

## Introduction

In recent years, biomedical research has been revolutionized by the use of large integrated databases such as ECHO [1], SEER-Medicare [2], and UK Biobank [3], as well as electronic health record (EHR) data [4], which connect clinical, environmental, genomic, and social data on an unprecedented scale. These datasets offer greater statistical power and diversity, enabling analysis of complex relationships. However, their size and complexity also reveal limitations in traditional statistical methods that also pose escalated threats to the validity of research utilizing such large datasets. Familiar tools such as p-values and confidence intervals may be misleading and meaningless. As datasets grow, sources of bias may become more pronounced, prompting a reassessment of valid inference in biomedical science [5–7].

Traditional study designs were created for situations with limited data, where random error was a major concern and hypothesis-testing helped manage uncertainty [8,9]. In large datasets, random error may become tiny, but systematic error may remain or even grow. Even minor differences can produce extremely low p-values [6,10]. Additionally, combining data from multiple sources leads to confounding that standard adjustments can’t fully resolve [11,12]. The result is a new paradox of large data: precision without validity. Small uncertainties may be estimated with great confidence, while the underlying effect remains conceptually mis-specified. With hundreds of variables, it becomes hard to distinguish confounders, mediators, and colliders (see Box 1: Glossary). Over-adjusting may block or create causal paths, resulting in statistically correct but causally irrelevant estimates [13,14]. Harmonizing data across cohorts introduces measurement errors and information loss [15,16], which in large datasets leads to biased results with deceptively precise confidence intervals [17]. Structural biases and site differences pose further major validity threats.

### Box 1: Glossary

Attenuation simulation: A simulation technique used to evaluate the extent to which measurement error attenuates an estimated association or effect.

Bland-Altman plot: A graphical method used to compare two measurement methods or techniques by plotting the differences between them against their averages.

Collider: A variable that is simultaneously influenced by two (or more) other variables; controlling for a collider should be avoided because it creates a spurious association between these other two variables.

Completed partially DAG: A graph that depicts an equivalence class of multiple causal DAGs (see below) that share conditional independence relationships, including directed arrows of causal relationships that are uniquely determined and identical across all valid DAGs in the equivalence class and undirected edges where the direction of causality varies across DAGs.

Confounder: A variable that is associated with an exposure and with an outcome but is not in the causal pathway from the exposure to the outcome; controlling for a confounder is essential to understand if there is a causal relationship.

Directed acyclic graph (DAG): A visual graph using arrows to show causal pathways between variables without any feedback loops.

Hierarchical modeling: A statistical model that accounts for data grouped in nested levels.

Inverse probability weighting: A method that weighs data points by the reciprocal of their treatment probability to create a synthetic sample where confounders are better balanced.

LASSO: A regression method for automatic variable selection that penalizes the absolute size of coefficients, shrinking to zero the least important ones and those that are highly correlated.

Latent-variable modeling: A modeling framework that estimates abstract, unobserved concepts using multiple directly observed variables.

Mediator: An intermediate variable that sits on the causal pathway from exposure to outcome.

Multiple-indicator modeling: A latent-variable approach that employs observed measures to represent a single underlying construct to reduce measurement error.

Propensity score: The probability that a subject receives a specific treatment based on their observed characteristics.

Regression calibration: A method that substitutes an error-prone predictor variable with its expected value which may be calculated from a validation sub-study.

Simulation-extrapolation (SIMEX): A simulation approach that adds baseline error to data, measures the trend of worsening bias, and then extrapolates backward to estimate the true effect without error.

Specification curve analysis: A method that runs every defensible alternative model combination to show how different analytical choices may affect the results.

Stepwise regression: An automated variable selection algorithm that adds or removes variables from a model one at a time based on some statistical criterion.

Trimming: The practice of dropping observations with extreme propensity scores to prevent data points with extremely high or extremely low probabilities from destabilizing the analysis.

Vibration of effects: The variation of a treatment effect when all possible analytical approaches, model choices, and/or sampling choices are considered.

Weight stabilization: A modification to inverse probability weights that multiplies them by the baseline probability of treatment, in order to avoid inflation of variance from extreme weights.

Large dataset analyses may have different purposes [18] that correspond to causal, descriptive, or predictive questions. Some problems such as confounding are relevant to causal questions, while other problems such as issues with p-values and measurement error affect large dataset research more broadly. Exploratory analyses would typically align mostly with descriptive estimands. However, it is relatively common for authors to indulge in causal language and spurious causal inferences even in these situations. Framing questions with clarity as to whether the pursued associations are causal or non-causal and using confidence intervals to present what associations the data and models are most compatible with (rather than whether or not there is an effect) may sometimes reduce some misinterpretations. A statistically significant result may not be necessarily clinically meaningful, and a non-significant result may not necessarily indicate no true association [19]. However, even when confidence intervals are used, persistent misinterpretations may remain a challenge [20,21].

Statistical and methodological threats to the validity of large dataset research are not just theoretical concerns for methodologists and data scientists. Large dataset research is increasingly informing medical policies and guidelines and there is a push for replacing randomized trials with the products of such large dataset analyses. Lower cost and the facility of obtaining results very quickly instead of waiting years for randomized trials to be done are touted as major advantages and often some non-randomized analyses are presented as equivalent if not superior to randomized trials [22]. However, analyses lacking validity may misinform and lead to suboptimal or detrimental health outcomes for individual patients, preventive strategies, and communities for medicine and public health decisions.

Big data debates tend to emphasize computational efficiency and accuracy over foundational issues like causation, bias, and measurement [23,24]. This paper outlines four main challenges: p-value inflation, confounding across sites, harmonization and measurement error, and causal identification with numerous covariates. Each challenge is explored with conceptual analysis and simulations, showing that bias often outweighs randomness in uncertainty. Along these lines, we also propose some guidance that may help make large-scale analytics more meaningful, credible, and reproducible. We use the term “large data” broadly to encompass datasets characterized by large sample size, high-dimensional variable measurement, or both. Such datasets often include extensive demographic, biological, social, and environmental information.

## P-value inflation and trivial effects

Hypothesis testing with p-values was built when data were scarce and experiments were expensive. In the large-data setting, that basic logic bends. Null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) asks, “If there were truly no effect, how surprising would these data be?”. But when the sample size is huge, almost any small departure from the null is “surprising” in the technical sense. Sampling variability shrinks, standard errors get tiny, and test statistics explode even when the underlying effect is biologically or clinically trivial. The result is p-value inflation, an overabundance of very small p-values that look persuasive but correspond to effect sizes that are too small to matter biologically or clinically [5,9]. With big data, the key question changes from "can we find it?" to "is it worth finding?"

There are at least three interrelated mechanisms behind this problem: true-but-not-worth-it effects get detected, spurious effects get detected, and too many effects may be pursued – and get detected. First, the test statistics for common models (t-tests, Wald tests, likelihood-ratio tests) grow roughly with $\sqrt{n}$, so doubling or tripling the sample size can turn a noisy, borderline association into one that is highly statistically significant for the same effect size [6,25,26].

Second, real-world large databases such as EHR-based cohorts, consortia, or multi-site studies, almost always have some model misspecification or leftover noise (e.g., unmeasured confounders, imperfect harmonization, nonlinearity). When working with very large samples, the model detects the misspecification and responds by producing low p-values for spurious effects.
